paper.code_data_availability: This paper uses confidential administrative data from Denmark. …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish administrative data / Danish register data

linkages: children are linked to both of their parents; children whose parents are not both identified are dropped
parental residence histories are used to require that both parents have lived in Denmark continuously since 1980

sample.universe: the full Danish birth cohorts of 1985, 1986 and 1987
selection_rules: both parents known to the researchers
both parents have lived in Denmark continuously since 1980
random split into an 80% training sample and a 20% test sample; all reported AUCs are evaluated on the test sample
sample.period: predictors from 1980 to birth (extended to birth + 1, 3 and 5 years in Section IV.D); outcomes measured between 2006 and 2019

construction_notes: Children are ordered by the outcome-specific cost they generate in adulthood and the top 20% of the distribution is defined as “at-risk” of that outcome (p. 8).

Eight outcomes: education (compulsory education only in 2018), income (bottom 20% equivalised disposable family income 2016-2017), social benefits (top 20% recipients, week 14/2006 - week 01/2019), criminal charges (ever charged as of 2017), placement (ever in placement or preventive measure as a child), hospitalizations (top 20% admissions 2006-2016), psychiatric condition (diagnosed as of 2016/2017), and a social burden (SB) indicator (top 20% of a single common factor of the seven outcomes from confirmatory factor analysis) -- Table 1, p. 34.

All continuous predictors are turned into discrete categorical variables; missing values are generally assigned to a separate category; a dummy is included for each category, giving 184 dummy variables (159 in the logit model, which omits the baseline category) -- p. 10.
80% training / 20% test split; tuning parameters of the machine learning methods chosen by 8-fold cross-validation on the training data -- p. 12.
Risk-score weights in Figure 4 are logit coefficients rescaled so the lowest possible score is 0 and the highest possible score is 100 -- p. 18.

Confidence intervals in Figure 1 and Figure 2 are 95% bootstrap intervals from 2,000 bootstrap samples of the test data, keeping the prediction function fixed; the bands in Figure 4 are 95% confidence bands based on robust standard errors.
The main text names no Danish register codes; data sources are listed in Table G.1 of the Online Appendix, which is not part of this PDF.
Table 2 (p. 34) reports polychoric correlations among the eight outcomes (0.16 to 0.90); these are descriptive and motivate the combination-of-outcomes analysis rather than being a tested claim.

claims.statement: Child and parental predictors available in the Danish registers at or before birth classify at-risk for the education outcome: compulsory education only out of sample with an AUC of 0.761.

treatment.label: set of child and parental predictors available in the Danish registers at or before the child's birth

definition.value: Child-level predictors (sex, county of residence at birth, region of origin, birth month, birth order) and parental predictors recorded separately for mother and father (income, wealth, educational attainment, occupation, working hours, age, marital status, hospitalizations, placements, criminal charges). All continuous predictors are discretized; missing values get their own category; 184 dummy variables in total (159 in the logit model, which omits the baseline category).

timing.value: measured at or before the child's birth (parental histories from 1980 onwards)

outcome.label: at-risk for the education outcome: compulsory education only

definition.value: Binary indicator for having completed compulsory education only, measured in 2018. Those with the outcome account for 100.0% of the total burden to society. Prevalence in the sample: 12.7% (Table 1).

timing.value: measured in adulthood; across the eight outcomes the age of measurement ranges from 28 to 33 years

units.value: area under the ROC curve (AUC) for out-of-sample classification on the 20% test sample; ranges from 0.5 (uninformed assignment) to 1

magnitude.interpretation: “Prediction works well for education, and also for criminal charges and foster care placement, with AUC values between 0.76 and 0.81” (p. 13); on the paper's own scale (p. 11) 0.761 is “fair”.

identification.source_of_variation: None: the paper is explicitly predictive rather than causal. It measures how well adult at-risk status can be classified out of sample from register variables observed at or before birth; the authors state that they do not observe treatment effects.

key_assumptions.assumption: The 20% hold-out test sample is exchangeable with the 80% training sample, so the AUC evaluated on it measures out-of-sample predictive accuracy for the cohort rather than in-sample fit.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 80/20 train-test split; tuning by 8-fold cross-validation on the training data; in-sample and out-of-sample fit compared and found very similar (Table G.8, Online Appendix)

key_assumptions.assumption: The relation between at-birth predictors and adult outcomes is stable across cohorts, so weights estimated on the 1985-1987 cohorts are informative for later cohorts.
key_assumptions.supported_by: model trained on one cohort and evaluated on another (Figure F.8, Online Appendix); the authors nonetheless note the predictors were recorded more than 30 years ago

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on both parents being known and having lived in Denmark continuously since 1980; children of unknown or recently-immigrated parents are excluded.

implies_edges.from: both parents known and continuously resident in Denmark since 1980

key_assumptions.assumption: Using the risk scores for targeting leaves the predictor-outcome relation unchanged (policy invariance). The authors state explicitly that this does not hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: none; the authors raise the Lucas critique as an unresolved caveat

identification.source_of_variation: None: the paper is explicitly predictive rather than causal. It measures how well adult at-risk status can be classified out of sample from register variables observed at or before birth; the authors state that they do not observe treatment effects.

key_assumptions.assumption: The 20% hold-out test sample is exchangeable with the 80% training sample, so the AUC evaluated on it measures out-of-sample predictive accuracy for the cohort rather than in-sample fit.
key_assumptions.supported_by: 80/20 train-test split; tuning by 8-fold cross-validation on the training data; in-sample and out-of-sample fit compared and found very similar (Table G.8, Online Appendix)

key_assumptions.assumption: The relation between at-birth predictors and adult outcomes is stable across cohorts, so weights estimated on the 1985-1987 cohorts are informative for later cohorts.
key_assumptions.supported_by: model trained on one cohort and evaluated on another (Figure F.8, Online Appendix); the authors nonetheless note the predictors were recorded more than 30 years ago

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on both parents being known and having lived in Denmark continuously since 1980; children of unknown or recently-immigrated parents are excluded.

implies_edges.from: both parents known and continuously resident in Denmark since 1980

key_assumptions.assumption: Using the risk scores for targeting leaves the predictor-outcome relation unchanged (policy invariance). The authors state explicitly that this does not hold.
key_assumptions.supported_by: none; the authors raise the Lucas critique as an unresolved caveat
